Coding alone, you lose time in small ways.
You fix the wrong file, or skip the tests.
And most AI tools wait to be asked,
or rewrite your code behind your back.
Pairing buddy is the person in the second chair.
It sits beside you in Neovim,
and speaks up only when it matters.
It never touches your files,
unless you hand it the wheel.
Two models share the work.
The Watcher is small and fast:
is this moment worth a word?
The Partner thinks before it answers, and writes the remark.
Install with two commands:
npm install, then pair setup.
Setup writes the config, and runs Pair in the background,
as a service.
Pair auth keeps your logins and keys in one file.
Choose an API key, type it once,
and it's never printed.
One local model can play both roles:
one number from the Watcher, without thinking,
and a Partner that thinks.
Pair doctor checks every part, down to whether the Partner really thinks,
and the sandbox Pair's commands run in.
Pair has three roles.
The Navigator watches and points.
The Scout also runs commands, in its own pane.
The Driver makes one change, then gives the wheel back.
Here is a webhook service in Go.
A delivery test is red,
and you start changing the backoff code.
But the failure doesn't name that file.
So Pair, the Navigator, reads the code first.
Then it speaks, under your line:
the shift is fine,
the worker gives up one attempt early.
Alt J jumps to the exact characters it means.
Searching in circles?
After three searches, Pair says where the thing is,
in the code's own word.
Pair context shows everything Pair knows on one card:
the goal from your board task,
git, your commands and buffers.
Builds and runs are read like tests:
a crash lands on its line in your code,
and so does a compiler error.
When you explore, each run of make gets a number,
next to the one before.
If a change did nothing, Pair says why.
Pair runs keeps the notebook,
and one key removes the print lines you added for the hunt.
Want the why?
Alt question mark gives the one idea worth keeping,
with a link.
A thought that can wait, waits:
a dot in the margin until your next save.
Tests are optional.
Set a test command,
and every save runs it in Pair's pane.
This fix breaks a queue test.
A regression, and you didn't even run the tests.
Pair says why, and offers its fix as ghost text:
dim, not in your file yet.
Alt Y takes it.
When a number finally moves the right way,
the statusline lights up once.
In a Markdown note, Pair thinks with you,
never for you:
a few marks in the margin.
An open question, two lines that clash,
what the code really does.
Alt D logs a decision,
and Pair tasks lists the work.
From an empty folder:
Pair new, and one sentence.
Three short questions, then a first slice that runs.
Hand it over, and it types two files.
Nothing is on disk until you save.
To hand over a change, say Pair drive, or just:
you take it.
Pair is the Driver, and you watch it type.
It tests your unsaved buffer, then hands back.
One undo takes it all away.
Changed your mind?
Any key takes the wheel back.
No test?
Say what you expect to see.
Pair runs the unsaved buffer in a scratch copy,
and checks the number.
Pair today lists everything Pair did today.
The U key undoes one of its edits,
even after yours.
Other agents' news waits for your next break.
Alt A goes to the one that needs you.
At the day's end, a debrief:
what's true, what's left, and tomorrow's first step.
Next morning, Neovim opens right there,
with one line on what's left.
And more.
Hold Alt T to ask aloud.
Soft sounds while you're away.
Your shell setup in Pair's pane, sandboxed.
Several Neovims, one session.
And without herdr, the terminal workspace,
Pair chat runs inside Neovim.
The keys to remember:
Alt J, Alt Y, Alt question mark,
Pair drive, and U.
Pair stays in the second chair.
